Learning Objectives
Define the structure and composition of various components of the intervertebral disk.
Define the motion segment and describe the blood and nerve supply of intervertebral disks.
Describe etiologic factors associated with disk degeneration.
Identify methods for assessing disk degeneration.
Recognize different classification schemes for disk degeneration.
Overview
Intervertebral disks are avascular fibrocartilaginous structures between the adjacent
vertebrae.
They allow for restricted movement between vertebrae while resisting spinal compression,
distributing the compressive load evenly on the adjacent vertebral bodies.1

Composition of the Intervertebral Disk
The nucleus pulposus, inner anulus fibrosus, outer anulus fibrosus, and cartilaginous end
plates (CEPs) are the four components that form the intervertebral disk.2
Nucleus Pulposus
The proteoglycans make up almost 20% to 60% of the dry weight of the nucleus,3 and water
constitutes 66% to 80% of its wet weight.4,5
Aggrecan is the key proteoglycan of the nucleus pulposus.
Takes the form of a large aggregate, forming a trivalent cross-linked structure, with the
aggrecan core protein decorated with sulfated glycosaminoglycans and hyaluronic acid
Linked with hyaluronan at the N-terminus and with the collagen fibrillar network and other
matrix components at the C-terminus6,7
Versican is another large aggregating proteoglycan; it is believed to play a role in cell
adhesion and proliferation.8
Type II collagen fibrils are the primary type of collagen in the nucleus; they make up 20% of the
dry weight.9,10 Type I collagen and elastin fibers are present in lesser amounts.11,12

Nucleus Pulposus
The nucleus pulposus, the central gelatinous area of the intervertebral disk, is highly
hydrophilic in nature. It is bounded peripherally by the lamellar structure of the anulus
fibrosus. It is mainly composed of proteoglycans, type II collagen fibrils, and elastin
fibers. Rounded chondrocyte-like cells also are present in the nucleus but at an
exceptionally low cell density.13 These cells are thought to originate from the inner
anulus14 or notochordal cells.15
The hydrophilic nature of nucleus pulposus is the result of proteoglycans, which attract
copious amounts of water because of the presence of a fixed negative charge. The
negative charge is provided by glycosaminoglycans, such as chondroitin sulphate,

forming proteoglycans.
Inner and Outer Anulus Fibrosus
Area between the nucleus pulposus and the peripheral anulus fibrosus
Mixed population of chondrocyte-like cells and fibroblasts16 lying within a fibrous matrix of
disorganized lamellae that appears discrete from the homogenous basophilic matrix of the
nucleus pulposus17
In this zone, the proteoglycan content decreases to approximately 20% to 35% of the dry
weight in the region.3
Outer Anulus Fibrosus
Lamellar in nature
Made up of highly organized parallel sheets of type I collagen fibers and collagen types II, III, V,
VI, IX, XII, and XIV in variable quantities18
The unique orientation of collagen fibers plays a tensile role during compressive loading.10
Small quantity of elastin fibers within the lamellae bind the structure together and provide
elasticity
The cells in the outer anulus, fibroblasts, are elongated and are aligned parallel to the collagen
fibers.19
Mesenchymal in origin
Contain actin microfilament and vimentin intermediate filaments that are important in
functions such as propagation of mechanical signals and mechanotransduction20,21
The fibers toward the inner aspect of the anulus fibrosus are anchored to the CEPs, whereas
the outer anulus fibrosus is anchored to the epiphyseal bone of the adjacent vertebrae by
Sharpey fibers.22
Proteoglycan content found in the outer anulus is only 10%;3 therefore, water content in the
outer anulus constitutes approximately 66% of wet weight, compared with 88% in the inner
anulus.23,24
Other Proteoglycans

One such protein is cartilage oligomeric matrix protein, which binds to collagen fibers to
regulate their assembly and maintain the structural integrity of the tissue.6,7
Fibronectin and cartilage intermediate layer protein are two other proteins present in the disk.
Precise role is unclear
Their presence and upregulation have been linked with degenerative disk disease.6,18

Other Proteoglycans
Several smaller proteoglycans in the disks—including biglycan, fibromodulin, decorin,
perlecan, and lumican18disk—are said to bind the collagen fibers and regulate their
assembly.25 These smaller proteoglycans also bind to the growth factors, especially
transforming growth factor,6 and aid in disk development and repair.
The extracellular matrix also contains a considerable amount of non-collagenous
proteins.
The CEP
The CEP is sandwiched between the intervertebral disk and the adjacent osseous vertebral end
plate.
Primary purpose is to provide a physical barrier between the hydrostatic nucleus and the
vertebral body and a pathway for the diffusion of nutrients from the capillaries of adjacent
marrow channels into the avascular disk tissue26
Hyaline in nature; variably composed of chondrocytes, collagen (mostly type II),
proteoglycans, and water
The only cells present in the CEP are chondrocytes, which are distributed throughout the
depth. The matrix surrounding the chondrocytes is mainly composed of hyaluronan,
proteoglycans, and type VI collagen.
Type II collagen fibrils are aligned parallel within the end plate, helping the CEP to withstand
high pressures within the adjacent disk nucleus.27
A small amount of types III, VI, IX, and X collagen is present throughout the matrix;28,29types
III and VI are found in the pericellular regions, and type IX is found in the territorial

matrix.28,30
Proteoglycans are enmeshed within the collagen fibril network and act to maintain the
hydration of the tissue.
Aggrecans, perlecan, and small leucine-rich proteoglycans such as fibromodulin and lumican
Large aggregating proteoglycans, aggrecan, provide much of the diffusion capacity to the
CEP.30
Anatomy of a Motion Segment
Each intervertebral disk along with its adjacent vertebrae, anterior and posterior longitudinal
ligaments, and the two facet joints form a motion segment, which has its own functional
importance.
Anterior longitudinal ligament
Thick, strong ligament at the anterior and anterolateral aspects of the vertebral bodies
Traverses from the atlas down to the sacrum
Rigidly attached with the vertebral bodies at its periphery
Deepest fibers merge with the intervertebral disk and extend from the body of one
vertebra to the disk, then to that of the neighboring vertebra.
Posterior longitudinal ligament
Lies posteriorly on the vertebral bodies
Extends from the atlas to the sacrum
Expands while passing over the disks, resembling an hourglass
Lateral fibers over the intervertebral disks are weaker than the strong central band and,
therefore, form a less well-enforced region for potential disk herniation.
At the posterior aspect, the adjacent vertebrae articulate through zygapophyseal or facet
joints; these joints are between the respective superior and inferior facets of the vertebral
articular processes and through the joints of the vertebral bodies.31
Blood and Nerve Supply of the Intervertebral Disks
Healthy adult intervertebral disks are avascular and aneural; however, a few blood vessels and
nerves are present around the peripheral anulus.
The blood vessels are derived from the external arteries supplying the adjacent vertebral
bodies.

Most of the nutrition of the disk comes from the adjacent vertebral end plate, which is highly
vascularized by the branches of spinal arteries.
Almost 80% of the nutrients are transported through the vertebral end plate route via the
process of diffusion or bulk flow.
Intervertebral Disk Degeneration
Disk degeneration can occur at any age; however, the risk increases with age.32
All disks are prone to age-related changes to a greater or lesser extent.33
Disks undergo a series of alterations as age progresses.
The first and foremost alteration appears to be reduction in water and proteoglycan content,
particularly in the nucleus pulposus.
With advancing age, the size of the proteoglycan molecule decreases, and the proportion of
non-aggregated proteoglycans increases.
The small fragments of the proteoglycans easily manage to leach out of the tissue, resulting
in dehydration of the disk.34
The dehydrated disk loses its hydrostatic ability, which greatly compromises its functional
role.
An increase in cross-linking and thickening of the collagen fibers occurs with age and may
cause retention of the denatured collagen in the disk, which reduces tissue strength.35
Altered metabolic activity occurs as viable cellular density declines in the aging disks.36,37
The spectrum of degeneration may incorporate all these age-related changes, even to an
exaggerated extent.38
Structural changes
Several key structural changes are observed irrespective of age, sex, and spinal level and are
recognized as signs of disk degeneration.1
Increase in fibrosity of the nucleus pulposus
Inward buckling of the inner anulus
Circumferential and anular radial tears responsible for radial bulge or herniation in many
patients
Reduction in disk height
Structural disruptions largely affect the mechanical functions of the disk, with adverse results.
Depressurization of the nucleus and concentrations of compressive stress in the anulus,39
which build up stress gradients within the disk matrix40

The response to this stress is premature senescence of cells41 and release of cytokines and
matrix-degrading enzymes from senescent cells,42 leading to a perpetual cascade of disk
degeneration.

Intervertebral Disk Degeneration
Disk degeneration may become a substantial health-related condition if pain develops. It
has a substantial association with many other clinical conditions, such as spinal stenosis,
disk prolapse or extrusion, and facet joint arthropathy.43,44
The intricate nature of the condition makes it challenging to define; however, the term
generally refers to the extensive morphologic, metabolic, biochemical, and functional
alterations in the disk.45
Etiologic Factors
Disk degeneration is a multifaceted disease, and despite decades of research, a clear picture
of causation has not yet emerged.
No single key contributor to the process of disk degeneration
Several factors that contribute
Arguably, the most important of these are mechanical, nutritional, and genetic factors; the
factor that is most detrimental to the disk remains unclear.
Environmental factors and lifestyle also play a critical role in the initiation and progression
of the disease.
An interaction effect of all potential risk factors likely contribute disk degeneration and may
be more personalized based on the individual.
Mechanical Factors
The intervertebral disks are cushion like structures that are meant to bear and evenly
distribute the compressive and bending stresses acting on the spine. Any change in the

loading pattern, intensity, and duration of stresses increases the risk of damage to the
disk.46,47
Excessive continuous static compression is believed to cause more damage to the
intervertebral disk than cyclic compression.48
Experiments performed on cadaver model motion segments showed disk mechanical failure
after prolonged compressive loading because of a break in the integrity of the end plate.
The fracture of the overlying end plate causes reduction in the hydrostatic pressure of the
nucleus, and resistance of compressive force is taken over by the anulus fibrosus,49 which
leads to the formation of stress peaks, particularly in the posterior anulus.50
A non-supporting nucleus gives way to an unstable inner anulus and buckles inward,49,51
leading to disruption of the remaining tissue.52
The pressure gradients and stress peaks break the inter- and intra-lamellar connections of the
anular fibers, and delamination and separation results in the formation of tears and fissures.53
Studies have suggested that prolapse of intervertebral disks may result from rotation and
bending motions in combination with compressive forces;54,55 these combined motions likely
produce anular radial fissures because of fatigue failure.55,56
Torsion, another vital component of loading, also is thought to increase the stress in the
posterolateral region and cause prolapse.57 The depressurized nucleus and fissured anulus of
the prolapsed disk is unable to resist the bending movement; an increase in the intra-lamellar
shear stress occurs, which causes additional mechanical disruption.38
All of these—asymmetric loading patterns, stress gradients, and tissue deformation—affect
the extracellular matrix and cellular organization of the disk.58
Studies have shown gene expression for aggrecan and type II collagen to be
downregulated,59,60 and an altered gene expression for certain matrix metalloproteinases
(MMPs) and tissue inhibitors of metalloproteinases occurs.46
Walter et al61 reported mechanically induced cell death and a shift toward catabolism because
of bending movements combined with compressive stress.
The disk with the altered metabolism and diminished cells experiences a chronic state of
distress that leads to subsequent disk degeneration.59
Altered loading pattern was reproduced in in vitro studies: injuries to the disks and the end
plates of human cadaver model motion segments and animal models were experimentally
induced to determine their effect on disk degeneration.51,62

The cut injury to the peripheral anulus of sheep disks affirmed the role of tears and fissures in
the process of degeneration.63
Findings of human cadaver model studies demonstrated the powerful part played by end plate
fracture in altering compressive load distribution compared with anular injuries.64
Reduction in the glycosaminoglycan content, upregulation of MMPs and cytokines, and
necrotic and apoptotic cell death are consequences of mechanically induced injuries to the
end plate.65,66
Similarly, a mechanically injured intervertebral disk causes upregulation of proteolytic
enzymes, loss of proteoglycan, and release of neurotrophins. Neurotrophins may promote
neuronal growth and sensitization, which may link disk degeneration and back pain.62
Nutrition
The intervertebral disk in adult humans is in a permanent state of nutritional paucity because
of its lack of vascularity.
Few blood vessels and nerves supply the margin of the peripheral anulus, and the remainder
of the disk depends on the capillaries and blood vessels present at the bone-cartilage end
plate junction for the nutritional support.67
The process of diffusion and fluid flow mainly are responsible for the transport of the
nutrients and wastes through the end plate route.68
Studies on the end plate have linked calcification and resorption of the CEP with
degeneration.69,70
Another factor disrupting the nutritional supply to the disk may be pathologic changes in
adjacent blood vessels through which nutrients diffuse.
Oxygen and glucose are the main nutrients required by the disk cells to stay alive.
Reduced pH decreases the rate of matrix component synthesis and activates the production
of proteases.71
A study using three-dimensional finite element analysis recorded reduction in cellular density
with nutritional deprivation,72 supporting the notion of a nutrition-related mechanism in disk
degeneration.

Nutrition

Oxygen and glucose are considered crucial for the wellbeing of intervertebral disk cells;
they reach the disk tissue via the process of diffusion. Metabolic wastes, such as lactic
acid, follow the same process but in a reverse manner.71 Transport occurs via the bony
end plate and the dense matrix of CEPs to reach the cells of the central disk tissue.71 Any
structural or biochemical change in the bony or cartilaginous counterparts of the end
plate may influence permeability or the diffusion process.71,73-75
Calcification and sclerosis of the bony end plate also were responsible for disk
degeneration, and studies have hypothesized that occlusion of the openings with
capillary buds may deprive the disk from nutrients.76 A 2011 investigation performed
after precise quantification of bone mineral density with the aid of micro-CT showed no
substantial association between bony end plate sclerosis and disk degeneration;77
however, an increase in porosity and permeability were observed with increasing disk
degeneration grades and age.78 These findings divert the attention toward the CEP, the
calcification of which may be a permeability barrier to the solute transport and facilitate
the process of degeneration.79
Lumbosacral spine segments are supplied by the branches of the abdominal aorta and
the internal iliac arteries. The disease process, such as atherosclerosis of the aorta or
segmental arteries, may compromise the nutrient supply to the disks.80,81 Constriction
of the blood capillaries because of smoking or short-term vibration also may be a
considerable factor in reducing diffusional transport across the disk.82
Glucose chiefly is used to provide energy, and lactic acid is produced as a byproduct. The
concentration of glucose is a sensitive parameter for identifying cell viability.83 With the
disturbance in the transport across the disk, the low levels of glucose and increased
accumulation of lactate compromise the viability of cells.
Genetics
Genetic association is another important factor in the process of disk degeneration.

Study findings have provided ample evidence of genetic links with disk herniation
characterized by sciatica.84-86
A positive family history is substantially association with the process of disk
degeneration.87,88
Being a multi-interdependent process, disk degeneration likely involves an interplay with
environmental factors.
The ongoing debate about gene–environment interactions was defined by Ottman89 in 1996
as “a different effect of an environmental exposure on disease risk in persons with gene
mutation or, equivalently, a different effect of a gene on disease risk in persons with different
environmental exposures.”89,90 This concept lead to the impression that individuals with
greater genetic predisposition to disk degeneration are more prone to respond to
environmental factors.
Among many features of disk degeneration, heritable features include disk height,
osteophytes, and annular bulging.91,92

Genetics
Polymorphism associated with the genes coding for the structural element of the
intervertebral disks also were studied and identified. These include genes coding for
collagen I (COL1A1),93 collagen IX (COL9A2 and COL9A3),94,95 collagen XI (COL11A2),96
aggrecan,97,98 cartilage intermediate layer protein,99 fibronectin,100 and
thrombospondins,101 as well as genes coding for catabolic enzymes, such as
MMP3,102,103 and inflammatory agents, such as interleukin 1.104 Several studies also
have established an association with polymorphisms in genes coding for the vitamin D
receptor105,106 and growth differentiating factor 5;107 however, these findings are not
consistent across all studies. The limitations may be attributed to differences in study
designs, ethnicity, sampling technique, and phenotype definitions, which weaken the
level of evidence for association.86
Despite a substantial amount of research conducted on the complex relationship
between genetics and disk degeneration, especially in the past two decades,

potential risk factors that may interact and lead to disk changes.
Other Environmental Factors

Other Environmental Factors
Risk of disk degeneration also has been attributed to various environmental and lifestyle
factors. Patients who are overweight or obese, smokers, physically inactive or overactive,
or who perform heavy labor have an increased risk of disk degeneration.
Obesity
Obesity is considered as well-known risk factor for low back pain,108 and disk degeneration is
one of the important key factors in this pain perception.109

Obesity
In a large population-based study involving 2,599 southern Chinese individuals,
investigators clearly illustrated that increased body mass index is a strong determinant
of disk degeneration. The authors also identified a positive association between body
mass index and the severity of disk degeneration and the number of levels involved.110
Many studies have depicted the role of various adipokines in the process of disk
degeneration.111,112 Adipokines, especially leptin, increase cellular proliferation,113 alter
cytoskeletal remodeling,112 and release MMP; therefore, they pose a high risk of aiding
in the degenerative process.114
The excessive body mass of an individual with obesity exerts a high compressive load,
and, concurrently, excessive abdominal fat shifts the body’s center of mass anteriorly,115

causing individuals with obesity to assume an extreme lordotic posture.116
Hyperextension of the lumbar spine, which occurs in patients with extreme lordotic
posture, causes concentration of compressive stress on the posterior anulus and
apophyseal joints and between the spinous processes.38 Shear force on the L5-S1 level
also is believed to be increased because this posture increases the inclination of the

Obesity and increased body mass index also are associated with decreased range of
motion at the lumbar level117 that may gradually limit the functional capability of the
spine118 and promote disk degeneration.
Smoking
Smoking also has been strongly linked to disk degeneration; research has shown that smoking
plays an integral part in this process.119,120

Smoking
Nicotine causes the production of carboxyhemoglobin and vasoconstriction, which
reduces oxygen transport and blood supply. The constriction of capillaries surrounding
the intervertebral disks may impair nutritional transport and lead to degeneration.121
The findings of in vitro experiments on cell cultures suggested reduced cell proliferation
and synthesis of extracellular matrix, especially glycosaminoglycan.122,123 In addition,
production of inflammatory cytokines after nicotine administration enhances the risk of
degeneration.124
Manual Labor
The potential association between some occupational hazards and disk degeneration also has
been emphasized in several studies.125-127

Manual Labor
Heavy mechanical labor may lead to many spine-related pathology, including
degeneration. Exposing the spine to frequent vibrations causes accumulation of fatigue
damage, leading to fatigue failure.38 The low metabolic environment of the
intervertebral disk is unable to cope with the repetitive microscopic damage to the
tissue, and an effective remodeling response is implausible.
Methods for Assessing the Phenotypes of Disk Degeneration

Methods for Assessing the Phenotypes of Disk Degeneration
Currently, the strong link between disk degeneration and low back pain generally is
accepted, and over many years, studies on animals and humans have developed and
refined several techniques to better understand of this process. Multiple in vitro and in
vivo methods are available to assess phenotypes of disk degeneration in laboratory and
clinical settings.
Gross Assessment
Direct visual assessment in cadaver model specimens can provide some valuable information
on the nature of lesions or defects that occur during life.
Gross morphologic examination of the disk is useful in identifying some obvious features
related to disk degeneration, which include changes in the consistency of the nucleus
pulposus, lamellar disorganization of anulus, occurrence and typing of tears, and
pigmentation of the disk.128
Disk height loss, osteophytes, and herniation are additional observations indicative of disk
degeneration.
Knowledge of disk morphology in relation to different histologic features in various injury
inflicted63 or mechanical models55,129 is a common practice in animal studies; it also is
applied in in vitro experiments using human cadaver model samples.

The established role of the end plate in disk degeneration has led scientists to evaluate this
structure with more emphasis.

Gross Assessment
A large-scale study macroscopically evaluated 1,148 vertebral end plates and recognized
four different types of lesions: Schmorl nodes, calcification, fractures, and erosions.130
The authors found Schmorl nodes, which can be easily appreciated via naked-eye
examination, to be the most common lesion. The second most common lesion was
erosions, which appeared as diffusive shallow breakdowns of the end plate. Fractures of
the end plate were identified as clefts or fissures with irregular margins. Calcification of
the vertebral end plates was the least common type of lesion.130 Calcification of the end
plate was not associated with any structural damage or cracks of the end plate; however,
it may impede disk nutrition by blocking the diffusion of nutrients.76 Exploring the link
between the end plate and gross morphologic changes in the disk via MRI, if available,
may help clarify many problems.
Animal and cadaver model studies do not allow for direct links between these changes
and back pain. This is a huge limitation of this technique; however, gross inspection is a
sensitive tool for identifying disk changes in vitro and may be used for academic
purposes.
Microscopy
Light microscopy with standard histologic techniques may reveal many distinguishing features
linked with the process of disk degeneration. More specific information about the composition
of the disk, inflammatory mediators, and the presence of blood vessels and nerves can be
obtained via immunostaining.
The use of electron microscopy to identify the disk ultrastructure in normal and degenerated
status131-133 and the use of recently introduced technologies, such as wide-field fluorescence,
confocal laser scanning microscopy, and three-dimensional live cell imaging,134,135 have
broadened the range of possible investigations. For a more thorough understanding of the

degenerative process, ultrastructural detail is studied under electron microscopy, focusing on
the pattern of collagen fibrils and cells of the anulus and the nucleus pulposus.
Use of fluorescent imaging and confocal microscopy have substantially increased knowledge
of various biochemical and inflammatory changes that may occur during the process of disk
degeneration.
Differential interface contrast microscopy also has proved highly effective in the study of disk
structural organization.136

Microscopy
This is another important and multidimensional in vitro technique, commonly practiced
in laboratory setup. Microscopic assessment provides thorough information on soft-
tissue structure and organization. Such level of detail may afford important knowledge
of the effects of aging, degeneration, and disease and, in some cases, may help inform
future treatment strategies.
Plain Radiography
Plain radiography often is the first imaging modality performed in the clinical setting because it
is inexpensive and easily accessible. It is used for the initial assessment of low back pain.
Radiography can demonstrate disk height and is unique in its ability to demonstrate weight-
bearing disk height and the effect of flexion and extension on the disk, revealing possible
vacuum disks (nitrogen gas formation in the disk due to negative pressure).
Additional findings observed on radiographs include the presence of osteophytes and sclerosis
of the end plate, which are associated with disk degeneration.137,138
With special reference to the vertebral end plate, morphologic assessments, involving an
evaluation of end plate shape and size, also can be performed; however, they cannot detect
any disk pathology and soft-tissue abnormality.
Computed Tomography
CT scan after diskography (injection of contrast into the disk) has fallen out of use because of
its dubious clinical utility in predicting outcomes postoperatively and its association with

increased disk disease at long-term follow-up. In addition, it is an expensive, invasive, and
painful procedure.
Although CT is faster to perform than MRI, it exposes patients to ionizing radiation and is
associated with poor soft-tissue differentiation, which makes it an inferior imaging modality for
investigation.

Computed Tomography
CT can capture bony details and is capable of imaging certain conditions, such as disk
herniations and spinal stenosis.139 It also can be used to visualize disk morphology and,
in combination with myelography, provide detailed images of nerve roots.140
Magnetic Resonance Imaging
Assessment of the disk usually is done on T2-weighted MRIs.
Signal intensity changes according to water content. Loss of water content reveals a black disk,
indicative of severe degeneration, whereas well-hydrated disks appear bright.141
Similarly, other associated changes, such as disk height loss, disk displacement, and annular
tears (formation of a high-intensity zone), also are very well recognized with MRI.142
Modic changes are MRI changes of the end plate and vertebral body marrow. These are
nonneoplastic subchondral bone marrow lesions that may involve various degrees of the
vertebral body.
Three main types of Modic changes
Type 1: inflammation
Type 2: fatty infiltration
Type 3: sclerosis and mixed types
Modic changes help distinguish between the acute and chronic phase of the disease and may
have clinical implications.143
MRI also can better detect other end plate phenotypes, such as Schmorl nodes and fractures,
compared with other clinical imaging modalities.144,145
Recently, T1-rho (spin lock) MRI has been used for musculoskeletal imaging. Its output can
identify early disk changes and biomarkers of disk degeneration. These techniques are

The introduction of fast low-angle shot imaging sequences and ultrashort time-to-echo

Use of fast low-angle shot MRI also is suitable for in vivo application and can reveal the three-
dimensional morphology of the CEP.149
The morphology of the CEP and defects, if any, can be detected via ultrashort time-to-echo
MRI.148This imaging modality enables visualization and provides complimentary information

Dynamic contrast-enhanced MRI also has been used for more quantitative approaches and
understanding in the analysis of disk degeneration.151,152 Additional improvements in this
diagnostic tool will aid in the early detection of disk changes.

Magnetic Resonance Imaging
MRI is considered the preferred imaging modality for evaluating disk degeneration and
severity.146 MRI is not only safer than various other imaging modalities from the
perspective of exposure to ionizing radiation but also excellent in soft-tissue
differentiation.
Classification of Disk Degeneration

Classification of Disk Degeneration
Many in vivo and in vitro grading systems of disk degeneration have been described in
the literature. The purpose of grading degenerative changes may be to compare the

Disk degeneration has been classified via imaging modalities including radiography,154,155
diskography,156,157 CT,158 and MRI157,159; these imaging modalities elucidate the degenerative
state of the disks, mainly in clinical settings. Conversely, in vitro studies allow for direct
macroscopic and microscopic evaluation of the disk and adjacent structures,128,160 which may
not coincide with in vivo assessment of the disk on MRI and other imaging modalities.
Well-known macroscopic128,161 and microscopic assessments160 and grading systems allow
for a more comprehensive analysis but have the least relevance clinically. Because of the
potential contribution of disk degeneration to back pain, a strong grading system based on
imaging modalities that can be applicable in the clinical setting is important.
Using MRI as a diagnostic tool, the widely used classification system described by Pfirrmann et
al159 is based on T2-weighted MRIs. Five grades are assigned according to the structure and
height of the disk, signal intensity changes, and distinction of the nucleus and anulus. This
grading system is associated with very good to excellent interobserver and intraobserver
reliability and also can be used for clinical and research purposes.153
Another grading system of disk degeneration via MRI was described by Schneiderman et al.157
This classification system is commonly used by researchers, and several studies have reported
correlations between back pain and severity of disk degeneration using this grading
scheme.162,163 This classification system focuses on signal intensity and classifies the
appearance of the disk into four categories.
No signal changes correspond with a normal disk.
A grade 3 disk has a hypointense nucleus pulposus with narrowed disk space.
A score of zero indicates all five levels are normal.
A maximum score of 15 is assigned if all levels have grade 3 degeneration.
